source.title: Comparative Analysis of LLM Abliteration Methods: A Cross-Architecture Evaluation

record.tranche_reason: The study applies several practical abliteration implementations and measures post-ablation refusals and benchmark performance. It tests effects relevant to removal, but does not reproduce the original per-layer, per-position activation intervention or test adding the direction.
record.gate_note: The study reports Heretic refusal outcomes and benchmark scores after abliteration, plus classifier-based refusal evaluations on a separate prompt set; these are recorded below. KL divergence and tool-compatibility results are not separate rows because they do not directly measure the claim's refusal behavior or general capability. Table 8's aggregate classifier comparison is omitted because per-model results are included.
record.test_reason: The study applies released weight-edit abliteration tools (Heretic, DECCP, ErisForge) to released instruct models. It reports post-edit refusal counts (Heretic, 8 models) and MMLU/GSM8K/HellaSwag against base scores (3 models). This bears on V2 and on V1's 'ablation removes refusal, abilities largely kept'. It does not isolate a single difference-in-means direction, does not test direction addition, and reports no pre-ablation refusal rates.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors frame this as a tool-selection study. Single-pass tools (ErisForge, DECCP) preserved benchmarks best, and Heretic had model-specific costs, notably Yi GSM8K −18.81 pp. They also report that GSM8K is the most sensitive benchmark and speculate it overlaps with refusal representations. Zephyr's low residual refusals are presented as consistent with H3 but needing more DPO-only models. In the ethics section they go further, claiming multi-stage alignment creates more distributed safety representations; their own data do not support this.
record.recipe_differences: Applies practical directional abliteration tools, including weight-based and decoder-layer approaches, using recommended defaults. It does not report the original per-layer/per-position projection experiment, a controlled single-direction comparison, or direction addition; Heretic uses Bayesian optimization and the tools differ in implementation.
record.method_sensitivity: Refusal outcomes varied across models. Capability impact varied by tool and model, with Heretic causing a large GSM8K drop on Yi-1.5-9B. Refusal estimates also differed substantially between the marker heuristic and the classifier on the separate prompt set.

fits_no_version.finding: Across eight Heretic-edited models, first-token KL divergence on harmless prompts correlates with remaining refusals (Pearson r=0.87, p=0.005).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models whose refusal is harder to ablate also suffer larger distribution shift from abliteration.

record.problems: Single experimental runs rather than multiple independent runs; refusal detection uses a marker heuristic that the paper reports can misclassify outputs; quantitative comparisons cover only subsets of models and tools; Zephyr has no base benchmark baseline; the alignment-training comparison is observational and includes only one DPO-only model. The paper notes that the benchmarks may miss other capability losses.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted KL-divergence results because token-distribution shift is not itself a refusal or capability measure named by the claim. Omitted tool-compatibility counts because they do not report the claimed behavioral effect. Omitted the aggregate classifier comparison in Appendix Table 8 because the per-model classifier results in Appendix Table 9 are recorded.

untested.parts: Whether a single difference-in-means direction is the mediator (Heretic searches layer ranges, weights and direction indices). Direction addition inducing refusal. Activation-level ablation. Refusal outcomes for DECCP and ErisForge. Pre-ablation refusal rates.
Refusal outcomes for DECCP, ErisForge and FailSpy. Pre-ablation refusal baselines. Models beyond 7–12B.

Not testable from this design. The alignment-category comparison has one DPO-only model, no pre-ablation refusal rates, and no controlled training intervention; Zephyr was trained without explicit safety data.

record.verdict_notes: V7 links and labels were removed. H3 rests on one DPO-only model, which was trained without explicit safety data, and no pre-ablation refusal rates are given, so low post-edit refusal is confounded with low initial refusal. Heretic optimises refusal count jointly with KL, so its refusal numbers are tuned outcomes, not a fixed ablation. No study rows are the original source. Benchmarks used 8-bit quantization; all results are single runs.

versions.untested_parts: Does not isolate whether one difference-in-means direction is the causal mediator, test projection from every layer and position, or test direction addition. Zephyr has no base-model benchmark scores.
Refusal outcomes are reported for Heretic, not for every weight-edit implementation or every released model; the study does not establish that all released-model weight edits remove refusal.

Training methods are compared across different models rather than controlled training interventions; the study does not test when refusal is trained or directly measure whether a single direction exists.

relation.reason: Its own post-edit refusal counts and capability deltas bear on whether weight-edit ablation removes refusal while keeping abilities.

tranche.reason: Applies released abliteration tools (Heretic, DECCP, ErisForge) with default settings to released instruct models. Measures refusal with a marker heuristic and capability with MMLU/GSM8K/HellaSwag. This is a different method on the same question.

source_check.notes: The paper's own check (Table 8, n=900) finds marker refusal precision is only 11.2% (marker ASR 72.2% vs classifier 95.7%), so r-row residual refusals are likely overstated. There is no pre-edit refusal rate; DECCP and ErisForge have no refusal measure. The text doesn't say whether Heretic's refusal-evaluation prompts are held out from its own optimization. Benchmarks ran in 8-bit and DECCP ran in 4-bit mode.

statements.correction: Heretic, 100 mlabonne/harmful_behaviors prompts, marker heuristic: 16/100 (DeepSeek-7B-chat, Mistral-7B-v0.3) to 54/100 (StableLM-2-12B); no pre-edit baseline. Table 8 (n=900, six abliterated models, separate prompts): marker ASR 72.2% vs classifier 95.7%.
statements.problem: Numbers right and the conditions name the marker heuristic. Note that the paper's own classifier cross-check suggests the marker counts overstate residual refusal.

statements.correction: 16–54/100 are marker-heuristic refusals after Heretic, no pre-edit rate. On separate generations from six abliterated models the classifier gives 84.7–100% non-refusal vs 50.0–86.7% by markers (Table 9). Marker refusal precision is 11.2% (Table 8).
statements.problem: 'Heretic leaves 16–54 of 100 refusals' is given as residual refusal with no judge qualifier. The counts come from a marker heuristic that the paper says under-estimates bypass, and there is no pre-edit baseline.

statements.correction: r04: Heretic on Llama-3.1-8B, 24/100 marker refusals, 76% ASR (95% CI 66.8–83.3), no pre-edit baseline. Table 9 classifier check for Llama-3.1-8B: 93.3% non-refusal vs 86.7% by markers (separate 150 prompts; tool not stated). At most limits_scope, not challenges.
statements.problem: Cites r04 under a 'challenges' label but doesn't name this study. r04 shows partial removal, not absent removal.

statements.correction: r02–r08: Heretic, 100 mlabonne/harmful_behaviors prompts, marker heuristic. c01–c06: existing UncensorBench generations, 150 prompts per model, six abliterated models (tool not stated), marker vs RoBERTa classifier on the same responses. Disclaimers count as non-refusal. DeepSeek-7B-chat 55.3% vs 84.7%; Mistral-7B-v0.3 76.7% vs 99.3%.
statements.problem: 'On the same generations' reads as the r02–r08 Heretic generations. The marker-vs-classifier comparison uses a separate set of generations.

statements.correction: r04: Heretic on Llama-3.1-8B, 24/100 marker refusals (76% ASR), no pre-edit baseline. Classifier check on separate generations gives 93.3% non-refusal.
statements.problem: Cites r04 but neither describes it nor lists it in the conflict group.

statements.correction: r05: Heretic (50 trials, defaults) on Qwen3-8B, 25/100 marker refusals (75% ASR, CI 65.7–82.5), no pre-edit baseline.
statements.problem: Cites r05 but doesn't describe this study.

statements.correction: r07: Heretic on Qwen2.5-7B, 42/100 marker refusals, 58% ASR (CI 48.2–67.2), KL 1.646, no pre-edit baseline. c06 (separate 150 prompts, tool not stated): marker 50.0% vs classifier 100.0% ASR (+50.0 pp).
statements.problem: 42/100 is right, but the statement omits that the same paper's classifier check gives Qwen2.5-7B 100% non-refusal. That is the largest judge gap in the paper and bears directly on this conflict.
